questions.question: What is the Singleton design pattern?
questions.title: Singleton pattern — only one instance of a class
questions.direct_answer: Singleton is a creational pattern whose intent is to control construction so one shared instance is used within a defined scope and provide access to it. A classic Java version uses a private constructor and static access, so its practical scope follows class loading rather than automatically covering every JVM, process, or cluster. Use it rarely: lifecycle ownership and explicit dependency injection are usually clearer than hidden global access.

sections.title: The Singleton Pattern: One Instance
sections.content:
The **Singleton pattern** controls a class's construction and exposes one shared instance within the scope of that implementation. A classic Java form uses a private constructor, a static field, and a static accessor.

The word “one” needs a boundary. Static state belongs to a loaded class, so multiple class loaders can hold separate instances, and separate JVM processes certainly do. Serialization, reflection, concurrency, and test isolation also affect hand-written implementations.

A shared resource does not automatically require the GoF global-access pattern. A dependency-injection container can own one object and pass it explicitly to consumers. That keeps dependencies visible and makes lifecycle and tests easier to control.

sections.title: Naive Singleton — not thread-safe
Thread-safe Singletons — DCL and the enum way
Singleton at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Intent|~controlled shared instance|one within a defined scope|managed construction|known access path
blue|Classic Java form|~static access|private constructor|static field|class-loading boundary
emerald|Concurrency|~safe publication|eager holder or correct locking|mutable state still synchronized|not solved by singleton alone
violet|Alternative|~dependency injection|container owns lifecycle|constructor shows dependency|scope is explicit

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No synchronization.** A plain `if (instance == null)` lets concurrent threads create multiple instances.
- **Forgetting `volatile`** in double-checked locking — without it, instruction reordering can publish a partially built object.
- **Mutable shared state.** Using a Singleton to pass data between unrelated classes is a global variable in disguise — it couples code and breaks tests.
- **Hand-rolling it inside Spring.** Spring already gives you singleton-scoped beans; manual `getInstance()` fights the framework.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Singleton controls construction so one shared instance is used within a defined scope
- A static Java implementation is scoped by class loading, not automatically by a cluster or every process
- Correct construction and publication do not make mutable operations thread-safe
- Global access can hide dependencies and share state between tests
- A container-managed dependency is often clearer than a hand-written `getInstance()`

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Singleton is a creational pattern that controls construction so callers use one shared instance within a defined scope. The classic Java form has a private constructor, a static field, and a static accessor. For example, `Configuration.getInstance()` may return one process-local configuration object, although an injected configuration service usually keeps that dependency clearer. I qualify the scope because static state follows the loaded class: another class loader or JVM process can have another instance. Lazy initialization also needs correct safe publication, and one safely created object can still have unsafe mutable methods. The main trade-off is global access, which hides dependencies and shares state across callers and tests.

questions.question: How does Spring Boot implement Singleton scope for beans?
questions.title: Spring bean singleton scope — Singleton pattern in Spring
questions.direct_answer: Spring's default singleton scope keeps one bean instance for each bean definition in one `ApplicationContext` and returns that managed instance to its consumers. It is not a JVM-wide GoF singleton and it does not use a public static `getInstance()`. Creation is container-managed, but thread safety of the bean's mutable behavior remains the application's responsibility.

sections.title: Spring Singleton Scope: Container-Managed
sections.content:
Spring's **singleton scope** means one managed instance per bean definition in an `ApplicationContext`. Consumers of that definition normally receive the same instance or a framework proxy that delegates to it. Another context can create another instance, so this is not a JVM-wide or cluster-wide singleton.

The container controls creation, dependency injection, lifecycle callbacks, and publication of the bean. That does not make every method or field thread-safe. Because a web application may call the same singleton bean concurrently, request-specific mutable state should stay in method data or a suitable narrower scope. Shared mutable state needs a deliberate concurrency design.

Unlike the classic GoF form, the class does not need a private constructor or static accessor. Its dependency remains visible through constructor injection and tests can construct the class with substitutes.

sections.title: Dangerous — mutable state in a singleton bean
Correct — stateless singleton, state in parameters
Spring Singleton Scope at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Default scope|~No annotation needed|one per bean definition|reused everywhere|container-managed
blue|Per-container|~Not per-JVM|one per ApplicationContext|test contexts may be reused|separate instances
emerald|Concurrency rule|~Keep request state out of shared fields|use parameters or a narrower scope|shared mutable state needs protection|locals may reference shared objects
violet|Not GoF|~Different mechanism|no getInstance|constructor injection|mockable in tests

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mutable fields in a singleton bean.** `currentUser`/`cartItems` are shared across all concurrent requests — classic race condition.
- **Thinking singleton means per-JVM.** It is per `ApplicationContext`; another context can create another instance, while Spring tests may reuse a cached context.
- **Hand-writing Singleton in Spring.** Don't add `getInstance()` — let the container manage the bean.
- **Prototype-in-singleton surprise.** Injecting a prototype into a singleton gives you one prototype frozen at singleton creation, not a fresh one per call (use `ObjectProvider`/lookup if you need fresh).

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Default Spring scope: one managed instance per bean definition per `ApplicationContext`
- It is not one object per JVM, process, or cluster
- Consumers may see a proxy while Spring manages the scoped target
- Container-managed creation does not make mutable business logic thread-safe
- Keep request data out of shared fields or choose a suitable scope/concurrency design

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Spring's default singleton scope means one managed instance for each bean definition in one `ApplicationContext`. Dependencies that refer to that definition normally receive the same object, sometimes through a framework proxy. This differs from a classic GoF singleton because the class needs no static field, private constructor, or `getInstance()` method; the container owns the lifecycle and dependencies remain explicit. The scope is not JVM-wide—another application context can create another instance. Spring creates and publishes the bean safely, but it does not make arbitrary mutable fields thread-safe. A service used by concurrent requests should not store request-specific data in shared fields, and any intentional shared mutable state needs synchronization or another suitable design.

questions.question: When should you use the Singleton pattern?
questions.title: When to use Singleton — appropriate use cases
questions.direct_answer: Use one shared instance when the application has a clearly owned service or resource whose lifecycle should match a defined container or process scope. Expensive creation alone is not enough; pools, caches, clients, and configuration objects need explicit lifecycle, concurrency, cleanup, and test boundaries. In Spring, prefer a singleton-scoped injected bean over a static global accessor, and never use shared fields for per-request or per-user state.

sections.title: Deciding When Singleton Adds Value
sections.content:
A shared instance is appropriate when one owner should manage a resource or service for a clear scope, such as one application context. Examples can include an HTTP client, connection pool, immutable configuration object, or cache—but each still needs its own concurrency, capacity, refresh, and shutdown design.

The GoF Singleton pattern adds global access as well as controlled construction. That global access often creates more coupling than the shared lifecycle itself requires. Dependency injection can provide one managed instance while keeping the dependency visible in constructors and replaceable in tests.

Do not use a singleton instance to hold the current user, cart, request, or transaction. Those values have a narrower lifecycle and concurrent callers would overwrite one another.

sections.title: Wrong — Singleton as a global mutable holder
Right — Singleton for a shared, read-only resource
Singleton: Yes vs No
sections.content:
amber|Good use|~Expensive resource|connection pool|config loaded once|cache / thread pool
blue|Good use|~Logically unique|one logger|one rule engine|consistent state
emerald|Bad use|~Global state|per-user / per-request data|shared mutable fields|hidden coupling
violet|In Spring|~Prefer beans|singleton-scoped @Bean|DI + testability|skip manual getInstance

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Sharing mutable state.** A `UserSessionManager` Singleton with `currentUserId` causes concurrent requests to overwrite each other.
- **Singleton for domain objects.** `Order`/`Cart`/`Product` are regular objects with many instances.
- **Dodging DI.** Calling `DiscountEngine.getInstance()` instead of injecting it hides the dependency and hurts tests.
- **Manual Singleton in Spring.** `@Service` singleton scope already provides this with better integration.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Define the scope and owner before choosing one shared instance
- Expensive construction alone does not solve lifecycle, cleanup, or concurrency
- Inject a container-managed shared service instead of hiding it behind static access when possible
- Shared mutable operations still need a concurrency design
- Per-user, per-request, and transaction data do not belong in application-wide fields

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I use one shared instance when a service or resource has one clear lifecycle owner for the application scope. For example, one Spring-managed HTTP client can share its connection pool across services and close that pool when the application context stops. The design still has to cover shutdown, concurrency, capacity, and refresh. I separate shared lifecycle from global access: constructor injection keeps the dependency visible and replaceable in tests. I do not put the current user, request, cart, or transaction in singleton fields because concurrent calls would share that state. Expensive creation is only a signal; the real decision is ownership, scope, and behavior.

questions.question: What are the problems with the Singleton pattern?
questions.title: Drawbacks of the Singleton pattern
questions.direct_answer: Singleton's problems: it **hides dependencies** behind static `getInstance()` (you can't see them in the constructor), makes **testing hard** via shared global state, often holds **global mutable state** needing tricky synchronization, and **violates SRP** by mixing logic with lifecycle control. **Spring's dependency injection** fixes these by moving lifecycle to the container and making dependencies explicit.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Hidden dependencies** — static `getInstance()` obscures what a class needs.
- **Testing difficulty** — global state couples tests and breaks isolation.
- **SRP violation** — logic plus lifecycle in one class.
- **Global mutable state** — needs careful synchronization.
- **Tight coupling** to the concrete class, not an interface.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Singleton has several serious problems that make it an anti-pattern in many situations. The biggest is hidden dependencies. When a service calls ConfigManager dot getInstance, you can't tell from the constructor what the class depends on — the dependency is invisible, which makes the code harder to understand and maintain. It also makes testing painful, because to test that service with fake configuration you can't easily inject a substitute; you'd have to use reflection or a tool like PowerMock, which are red flags. Another problem is global mutable state. If the Singleton has fields that change, like the current user or active session, multiple threads access and modify that shared state concurrently, so you need complex synchronization and it's easy to introduce race conditions. Singleton also violates the Single Responsibility Principle, because the class is responsible both for its business logic and for managing its own lifecycle — two different concerns mixed together. And in Spring applications, hand-rolling a Singleton fights the framework, since Spring already gives you singleton-scoped beans with the benefits and none of the drawbacks. The key insight to leave them with is that dependency injection solves Singleton's problems by externalizing lifecycle management: you still get a single instance when you want one, but the dependency is explicit in the constructor and easy to mock, so your tests stay isolated and deterministic.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**Singleton** is a creational pattern that guarantees a class has exactly **one instance** and gives a global access point to it.

You enforce it with a **private constructor**, a **static instance field**, and a static `getInstance()`.

It's for shared resources — connection pools, config, logging — where extra instances waste resources or split state. The fresher trap: it must be **thread-safe**.

Writing a plain null-check without synchronization, letting two threads create two instances

sections.title: Hard to test — hidden dependency + global state
Fixed — inject the dependency, mock it freely
Singleton's Trade-offs
sections.content:
amber|Hidden dependencies|~getInstance everywhere|invisible in constructor|hard to follow|hard to mock
blue|Testing pain|~Global state|tests share it|order-dependent|flaky
emerald|SRP violation|~Two jobs|business logic|+ lifecycle control|harder to change
violet|The fix|~Spring DI|container owns lifecycle|explicit dependencies|mockable in tests

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating Singleton as a default.** Most objects should have many instances; not everything needs to be unique.
- **Tests that share Singleton state** — they become order-dependent and flaky.
- **Ignoring Spring alternatives** — manual `getInstance()` in a Spring app reinvents what `@Service` already does, worse.
- **Mutable fields in a Singleton** — concurrency bugs across threads serving different users.

sections.title: When this choice makes sense
sections.content: Use Singleton when a resource is **expensive to create** or must be **logically unique**: connection pools, config loaded once, logging, caches, thread pools. **Don't** use it to pass state between unrelated classes — that's global-state abuse that creates hidden coupling and race conditions. In Spring, prefer a singleton-scoped bean over a hand-rolled `getInstance()`.

questions.question: What is the enum-based Singleton in Java and why is it preferred?
questions.title: Enum Singleton — the safest Singleton in Java
questions.direct_answer: An enum singleton declares one enum constant, such as `INSTANCE`. Java initializes each enum class safely, normal reflective construction of enum constants is prohibited, and serialization resolves the named constant instead of creating a normal new object. The guarantee is still per loaded enum class, so separate class loaders or JVMs can have separate instances. It is a compact choice when static global access is genuinely intended, but it is eager on first enum-class initialization and less flexible than dependency injection.

sections.title: Enum Singleton: The Java Way
sections.content:
An enum singleton is an enum type with one declared constant. Java's class-initialization rules publish the constant safely, reflective `Constructor.newInstance` cannot create enum objects, and standard Java serialization identifies the enum constant by name instead of serializing normal instance state.

These guarantees remove several bugs found in hand-written static singletons, but they do not create one object across class loaders, JVM processes, or machines. The instance is created when that enum class is initialized, and an enum cannot extend another class.

Use it when a process-local static access point is deliberately part of the design. In code that already uses dependency injection, a container-managed bean is usually easier to configure, replace, and isolate in tests.

sections.title: Classic Singleton — breakable by reflection
Enum Singleton — reflection and serialization safe
Why Enum Singleton Wins
sections.content:
amber|Thread-safe|~For free|class loading guarantees it|no volatile|no synchronized
blue|Serialization-safe|~For free|same instance on deserialize|no readResolve|JVM handles it
emerald|Reflection-safe|~For free|enum constructor blocked|can't be broken|setAccessible fails
violet|Limits|~Know them|eager initialization|can't extend a class|can implement interfaces

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using it inside Spring.** You lose DI, AOP proxies, and easy mocking — prefer singleton beans.
- **Trying to extend a class.** Enums can't; if you need inheritance use the holder pattern or a bean.
- **Assuming mutable state is safe.** Thread-safe *initialization* doesn't make mutable fields thread-safe — you'd still need synchronization.
- **Forgetting it's eager.** The instance is built at class load; if creation is expensive and may be unused, consider the Bill Pugh holder pattern for laziness.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Declare one enum enum constant such as `INSTANCE`
- Java class initialization provides safe construction and publication
- Normal reflection cannot construct an enum constant; serialization resolves its declared name
- The scope is per loaded enum class, not across class loaders, processes, or a cluster
- Prefer dependency injection when configurable lifecycle and test substitution matter

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: An enum singleton is an enum with one constant, commonly `INSTANCE`. It is concise because Java handles safe class initialization, normal reflective construction of enum constants is prohibited, and standard serialization resolves the declared constant instead of creating a separate ordinary object. I still qualify the scope: another class loader or JVM process can load its own enum class and instance. The constant is created when the enum class is initialized, and the enum cannot extend another class. It is a good compact implementation when static global access is truly required, but in a Spring design I often prefer an injected managed bean because configuration, lifecycle, and tests are more flexible.
